questions.text: (a) “Human beings were able to develop technology after they developed better understanding of natural laws.” Evaluate the statement in the context of naturalization of humans.

answer.text: (a) Human beings developed technology after developing a better understanding of natural laws: technology indicates the level of cultural development of society; understanding of concepts of friction and heat helped discover fire; understanding of secrets of DNA and genetics enables conquering diseases; laws of aerodynamics are used to develop faster planes; knowledge about nature is extremely important to develop technology, and technology loosens the shackles of environment on human beings; in early stages of interaction with their natural environment humans were greatly influenced by it. (Any three points to be analyzed)

questions.text: (b) “The imprints of human activities are created everywhere.” Evaluate the statement in context of humanization of nature.
questions.topic: Humanisation of Nature: Possibilism and Neo-determinism

answer.text: (b) The imprints of human activities are created everywhere: people begin to understand their environment and the forces of nature with the passage of time; with social and cultural development humans develop better and more efficient technology; they move from a state of necessity to a state of freedom; they create possibilities with resources obtained from the environment; human activities create cultural landscape e.g. health resorts on highlands, huge urban sprawls, fields, orchards and pastures in plains and rolling hills, ports, oceanic routes on oceanic surface and satellites. (Any three points to be evaluated)

questions.text: “The strong forces of nature used to control the human activities in the primitive societies.” Examine the statement.

answer.text: The strong forces of nature used to control human activities in primitive societies: in the early stages of development, primitive societies were controlled by forces of nature; at that stage, the level of technology was very low; they were afraid of the fury of nature and worshipped it; the humans were completely naturalised. (Any three points to be examined)

questions.text: “The basic emphasis is laid on the relationship between nature and human beings in all geographical studies.” Explain the statement.

answer.text: The Earth is the home of mankind; all natural phenomena that take place affect human beings; humans also modify the natural environment; there is inter-relationship between nature and man. (To be assessed as a whole)

questions.text: “Human Geography is the study of the changing relationship between the unresting man and unstable earth.” Support the statement.

answer.text: Natural elements such as landform, soils, climate, etc. keep on changing with time and space; humans also respond to such changes accordingly; as natural phenomena change, human activities change accordingly; nature and human beings are inseparable elements and should be seen holistically; humans have to adjust with the changing nature of the Earth; this correlation has been and will remain in future. (Any three points to be explained)

questions.text: (a) Explain with example the concept of environmental determinism.

answer.text: (a) Environmental determinism: the interaction between primitive human society and strong forces of nature is known as environmental determinism — human beings listened to nature, were afraid of its fury, and worshipped nature. Examples: direct relationship of a household belonging to an economically primitive society with nature; nature is the powerful force, worshipped, revered and conserved; there is a direct dependence of human beings on nature for resources which sustained them (any three points to be explained).

questions.text: (b) “The dichotomy between physical and human is not a very valid one.” Explain the statement with example.

answer.text: (b) The dichotomy between physical and human is not a very valid one because nature and human are inseparable elements; it should be seen holistically; both physical and human phenomena are described in metaphors using symbols from human anatomy. Examples: 'mouth' of the river, 'neck' of isthmus, 'profile' of the soil, 'face' of the earth, 'eye' of the storm, etc.; networks of roads, railways and waterways have been described as 'arteries of circulation'; regions, villages, towns have been described as 'organisms' (any three points to be explained).

questions.text: (a) How has the use of technology helped people to overcome nature’s obstacles ? Analyse.
questions.topic: Humanisation of Nature: Possibilism and Neo-determinism

answer.text: (a) Use of technology helped people overcome nature's obstacles: people begin to understand their environment and the forces of nature with the passage of time; with social and cultural development, humans develop better and more efficient technology; they move from a state of necessity to a state of freedom, creating possibilities with the resources obtained from the environment; it is technology that has allowed people (e.g. of Trondheim) to overcome the constraints imposed by nature — for example, health resorts on the highlands, huge urban sprawls, ports on the coasts, satellites in space, etc. (any three points to be analysed).

questions.text: (b) How does neo-determinism try to achieve balance between two concepts of man – environment relationship ? Analyse.
questions.topic: Humanisation of Nature: Possibilism and Neo-determinism

answer.text: (b) Neo-determinism tries to achieve a balance between the two concepts of man-environment relationship: it shows that neither is there a situation of absolute necessity nor a condition of absolute freedom; it means that human beings can conquer nature by obeying it; humans have to respond to the 'red signals' and can proceed in their pursuits of development only when nature permits the modification; possibilities can be created within the limits which do not damage the environment — there is no free run without accidents (any three points to be analysed).

questions.text: “Neo-determinism attempts to bring a balance between the two concepts of human-environment relationship.” Examine the statement with examples.
questions.topic: Humanisation of Nature: Possibilism and Neo-determinism

answer.text: Neo-determinism attempts to bring a balance between the two concepts of human-environment relationship (any three points to be examined): the concept shows that neither is there a situation of absolute necessity nor is there a condition of absolute freedom; it means human beings can conquer nature by obeying it; they have to respond to red signals and can proceed in their pursuits of development when nature permits the modification; possibilities can be created within the limits which do not damage the environment; in cities, traffic is regulated by lights on the cross roads — red light means stop, amber light provides a gap between red and green lights to get set, and green light means go.

questions.text: Explain the concept of ‘Humanisation of Nature’ by giving examples.
questions.topic: Humanisation of Nature: Possibilism and Neo-determinism

answer.text: Concept of ‘Humanisation of Nature’ (any three points to be explained): the people begin to understand their environment and the forces of nature with the passage of time; with social and cultural development, human beings develop better and more efficient technology; they move from a state of necessity to a state of freedom; they create possibilities with the resources obtained from environment — the human activities create cultural landscape; the imprints of human activities are created everywhere — health resorts on highlands, huge urban sprawls, fields, orchards and pastures in plains and rolling hills, ports on the coasts, oceanic routes on the oceanic surface and satellites in the space.

questions.text: (a) “Nature and human are inseparable elements in all geographical studies.” Examine the statement.

answer.text: (a) “Nature and human are inseparable elements in all geographical studies” (any three points to be examined): all geographical studies emphasize on the study of nature and human beings; it is interesting to note that both physical and human phenomena are described using symbols from the human anatomy; regions, villages, towns have been described as the state/country as a living organism; network of roads, railways and waterways have often been described as arteries of circulation.

questions.text: (b) Examine the main aspects of environmental determinism.

answer.text: (b) Main aspects of environmental determinism (any three points to be examined): there is always interaction between humans and natural phenomena; primitive societies were intimately dependent on nature for food and other resources; we can imagine the presence of a naturalized human who listened to nature, was afraid of its fury and worshipped it; strong forces of nature always guided human activities; this relation was termed as environmental determinism.

questions.text: (a) “Nature and human are intricately inter-wined.” Analyse the statement.

answer.text: (a) Nature and human are intricately inter-twined: (i) Nature and humans are inseparable elements and should be seen holistically. (ii) Both physical and human phenomena are described in metaphors using symbols from human anatomy. (iii) Face of the earth, eye of the storm, mouth of the river, snout of the glacier are some examples. (iv) Similarly, regions, villages, towns have been described as 'Organism'. Networks of roads, railways and waterways have been described as arteries of circulation. (any three points, or any other relevant point)

questions.text: (b) “Human beings utilize the opportunities provided by nature.” Analyse the statement.
questions.topic: Humanisation of Nature: Possibilism and Neo-determinism

answer.text: (b) Human beings utilize the opportunities provided by nature: (i) Humans create possibilities with resources obtained from the environment. (ii) Humans move from the state of necessity to the state of freedom. (iii) Human activity creates a cultural landscape. (iv) The imprints of human activities are everywhere - health resorts on highlands, huge urban sprawls, fields, orchards and pastures in plains and rolling hills, ports on the coasts, oceanic routes on the oceanic surface and satellites in space. (any three points, or any other relevant point)

questions.text: (a) “Human geography is a highly interdisciplinary subject.” Analyse the statement.
questions.topic: Fields and Sub-fields of Human Geography

answer.text: (a) Human geography is a highly interdisciplinary subject: (i) Human Geography attempts to explain the relationship between all elements of human life and the space they occur over. (ii) It assumes a highly interdisciplinary nature. (iii) It develops close interface with other sister disciplines in social sciences in order to understand and explain human elements on the surface of the earth. (iv) With the expansion of knowledge, new sub-fields emerge, and it has also happened to human geography. (v) For example, Urban Geography has an interdisciplinary connection with Urban Studies and Planning, or Population Geography has an interdisciplinary connection with Demography. (any three points, or any other relevant point)

questions.text: (b) “Human geography tries to explain the relationship of human beings with the physical environs of their occupance.” Analyse the statement.

answer.text: (b) Human geography and the physical environs of human occupance: (i) Human Geography studies the inter-relationship between the physical environment and socio-cultural environment created by human beings through mutual interaction with each other. (ii) Physical environment like landforms, soil, flora and fauna, water, climate etc. provide a stage for different activities. (iii) Human beings have made houses, cities, villages, ports, farms, elements of daily use and other elements of material culture by using the resources provided by the physical environment. (iv) While the physical environment has been greatly modified by human beings, in turn human lives also have been impacted. (any three points, or any other relevant point)

questions.text: (a) Examine the concept of naturalisation of humans.

answer.text: (a) The concept of naturalisation of humans: (i) In early stages of their interaction with the natural environment, humans were greatly influenced by it. (ii) They adapted to the dictates of nature. (iii) Human beings used to live in complete harmony with their natural environment. (iv) Human beings are directly dependent on nature for their sustenance. (v) The level of technology was very low, and the stage of human social development was primitive. (vi) The interaction between primitive human society and strong forces of nature is called environmental determinism. (vii) Human beings listened to nature and were completely naturalised; they feared nature's fury and worshipped it. (viii) Nature is considered a powerful force - worshipped, revered and conserved. (any three points, or any other relevant point)

questions.text: (b) Examine the humanistic approach of human geography.
questions.topic: Human Geography through the Corridors of Time

answer.text: (b) The humanistic approach of human geography: (i) It is also known as the welfare school of thought. (ii) This new school emerged in the 1970s as a result of discontentment with the quantitative revolution. (iii) It was mainly concerned with the different aspects of social well-being of the people. (iv) Housing, health and education are its main aspects. (v) It is taught at the postgraduate level as Geography of Social Well-being. (any three points, or any other relevant point)

questions.text: Read the passage carefully and answer the questions no. 15 to 17. Relation Between Humans and their Physical Environment -- You are already aware of the fact that the core concern of geography as a discipline is to understand the earth as home of human beings and to study all those elements, which have sustained them. questions.chapter: The World Population: Distribution, Density and Growth
questions.text: Read the case study given below and answer Q. No. 15 to 17. Stages of Demographic Transition Theory -- The first stage of demographic transition theory has high fertility and high mortality because people reproduce more to compensate for the deaths due to epidemics and variable food supply. The population growth is slow and most of the people are engaged in agriculture, where large families are an asset. Life expectancy is low, people are mostly illiterate and have low levels of technology. Two hundred years ago, all the countries of the world were in this stage. Fertility remains high in the beginning of second stage but it declines with time. This is accompanied by reduced mortality rate. Improvements in sanitation and health conditions lead to decline in mortality. Because of this gap, the net addition to population is high. In the last stage, both fertility and mortality decline considerably. The population is either stable or grows slowly. The population becomes urbanized, literate and has high technical know-how and deliberately controls the family size. This shows that human beings are extremely flexible and are able to adjust their fertility. In the present day, different countries are at different stages of demographic transition. Which among the following stage/stages has/have high growth of population ?

answer.text: Only the second stage

questions.chapter: The World Population: Distribution, Density and Growth
questions.text: Define the terms immigration and emigration. Analyse demographic transitions theory in the world.

answer.text: Immigration: Migrants who move into a new place are called immigrants. Emigration: Migrants who move out of a place are called emigrants. Demographic Transition Theory: (i) It can be used to describe and predict the future population of any area. (ii) The theory tells us that the population of any region changes from high births and high deaths to low births and low deaths as society progresses from a rural, agrarian, illiterate state to an urban, industrial, literate one. (iii) The first stage has high fertility and high mortality, with slow population growth due to epidemics and variable food supply. (iv) The second stage is marked by high fertility in the beginning which declines with time, and reduced mortality rate due to improvement in sanitation and health. (v) In the last stage, both fertility and mortality decline considerably, and population is either stable or grows slowly due to urbanised and literate population. (any three points, or any other relevant point)

questions.chapter: The World Population: Distribution, Density and Growth
questions.text: (a) Examine the role of climate, water availability and soil fertility on the distribution of world population.
questions.topic: Factors Influencing the Distribution of Population

answer.text: (a) Role of climate, water availability and soil fertility on distribution of world population: Availability of water - water is the most important factor in life, so people prefer to live in areas where freshwater is easily available, used for drinking, bathing, cooking, cattle, crops, industries and navigation; river valleys are among the most densely populated areas of the world. Climate - an extreme climate such as very hot or cold deserts is uncomfortable for human habitation; areas with a comfortable climate, without much seasonal variation, attract more people; areas with very heavy rainfall or extreme harsh climates have low populations; Mediterranean regions were inhabited from early periods in history due to their pleasant climate. Soils - fertile soils are important for agricultural and allied activities; areas with fertile loamy soils have more people living in them as these can support intensive agriculture.

questions.chapter: The World Population: Distribution, Density and Growth
questions.text: (b) Examine three stages of demographic transition theory.

answer.text: (b) Three stages of demographic transition theory: The first stage has high fertility and high mortality because people reproduce more to compensate for deaths due to epidemics and variable food supply; population growth is slow, most people are engaged in agriculture where large families are an asset; life expectancy is low, people are mostly illiterate and have low levels of technology; two hundred years ago all countries of the world were in this stage. In the beginning of the second stage, fertility remains high but declines with time, accompanied by a reduced mortality rate due to improvements in sanitation and health conditions; because of this gap, the net addition to population is high. In the last stage, both fertility and mortality decline considerably; the population is either stable or grows slowly; the population becomes urbanized, literate, has high technical know-how, and deliberately controls family size.

answer.text: Analyse any five factors influencing the distribution of the world population. Geographical factors - Availability of water: essential for life (drinking, bathing, cooking), crucial for agriculture, livestock, industries and transportation (navigation); river valleys are densely populated. Landforms: people prefer flat plains and gentle slopes, favourable for agriculture, road construction and industrial development; mountainous and hilly areas are less populated due to uneven land - the Ganga plains are densely populated while Himalayan mountain zones are sparsely populated. Climate: extreme climates (hot or cold deserts) are unfavourable for habitation; comfortable climates with minimal seasonal variation attract more people; Mediterranean regions attract population due to their pleasant climate. Soils: fertile soils are important for agricultural and allied activities; areas with fertile loamy soils have more people living on them. Economic factors - Minerals: mining and industrial activities generate employment as mineral deposits attract industries; skilled and semi-skilled workers move to these areas, making them densely populated - the Katanga-Zambia copper belt is one such example. Urbanisation: cities offer better employment, educational and medical facilities, and better transport and communication, leading to rural-urban migration; mega cities continue to attract large numbers of migrants every year. Industrialisation: industrial belts provide job opportunities and attract large numbers of people - the Kobe-Osaka region of Japan is thickly populated because of the presence of many industries. Social and cultural factors: places of religious or cultural significance attract population; social and political unrest cause people to move away; government incentives can influence population distribution in sparsely populated or overcrowded areas. (any five points, or any other relevant point)

questions.topic: Factors Influencing the Distribution of Population

answer.text: (a) Factors affecting the distribution of population in the world: (i) Availability of water - water is the most important factor for life, so people prefer to live where fresh water is easily available. Landforms - people prefer living on flat plains and gentle slopes, as such areas are favourable for crop production and for building roads and industries. (ii) Climate - an extreme climate such as very hot or cold deserts is uncomfortable for human habitation; areas with a comfortable climate, without much seasonal variation, attract more people; areas with very heavy rainfall or extreme and harsh climates have low population. (iii) Soils - fertile soils are important for agricultural and allied activities, so areas with fertile loamy soils have more people living on them as these can support intensive agriculture. (iv) Minerals - areas with mineral deposits attract industries; mining and industrial activities generate employment. (v) Urbanisation - cities offer better employment opportunities, educational and medical facilities, and better means of transport and communication; good civic amenities and the attraction of city life draw people to cities. (vi) Industrialisation - industrial belts provide job opportunities and attract large numbers of people, including factory workers as well as transport operators, shopkeepers, bank employees, doctors, teachers and other service providers. (vii) Social and cultural factors - some places attract more people due to religious or cultural significance, while people move away from places with social and political unrest; governments often offer incentives to live in sparsely populated areas or move away from overcrowded places. (any five points, or any other relevant point)

questions.text: (b) Define ‘migration’. Differentiate between pull and push factors of population migration.

answer.text: (b) Migration is the movement of people from the place of origin to the place of destination. Difference between pull and push factors: (i) push factors operate at the place of origin, and pull factors at the place of destination. (ii) unemployment, poor living conditions, political turmoil, unpleasant climate, natural disasters, epidemics and socio-economic backwardness are push factors, whereas better job opportunities and living conditions, peace and stability, security of life and property, and pleasant climate are pull factors. (iii) inadequate infrastructure (e.g. transportation, housing, utilities) can diminish quality of life, whereas well-developed infrastructure and access to services enhance the attractiveness of a destination. (iv) social strife, ethnic or racial discrimination and lack of community support push people to search for more favourable environments. (v) regions offering advanced medical facilities and reputable educational institutions are attractive to families and individuals alike. (any four points of difference, or any other relevant point)

Explain the concept of ‘human development’. Examine four approaches to human development.

answer.text: Human Development is the development that enlarges people's choices and improves their lives; people are central to all development as per this concept. Four approaches to human development: (i) Income approach - one of the oldest approaches; human development is seen as linked to income, the idea being that the level of income reflects the level of freedom an individual enjoys; higher the level of income, higher the level of human development. (ii) Welfare approach - looks at human beings as beneficiaries or targets of all development activities; argues for higher government expenditure on education, health, social and other amenities; people are not participants in development but only passive recipients; the government is responsible for increasing levels of human development by maximizing expenditure on welfare. (iii) Basic needs approach - initially proposed by the International Labour Organization; six basic needs - health, education, food, water supply, sanitation and housing - were identified; the question of human choices is ignored, the emphasis is on provision of basic needs. (iv) Capability approach - associated with Professor Amartya Sen; building human capabilities in the areas of health, education and access to resources is the key to increasing human development.

(iv) Development cannot take place unless there is an increment or addition to the existing conditions. (v) Development occurs when positive growth takes place, yet positive growth does not lead to development - development occurs when there is a positive change in quality. (vi) For example, if the population of a city grows from one lakh to two lakhs over a period of time, it shows the city has grown; however, if facilities like housing, provision of basic services and other characteristics remain the same, then this growth has not been accompanied by development. questions.text: Read the given passage carefully and answer the questions that follow : Methods of Mining -- Depending on the mode of occurrence and the nature of the ore, mining is of two types : surface and underground mining. The surface mining also known as open-cast mining is the easiest and the cheapest way of mining minerals that occur close to the surface. Overhead costs such as safety precautions and equipment are relatively low in this method. The output is both large and rapid. When the ore lies deep below the surface, underground mining method (shaft method) has to be used. In this method, vertical shafts have to be sunk, from where underground galleries radiate to reach the minerals. Minerals are extracted and transported to the surface through these passages. It requires specially designed lifts, drills, haulage vehicles, ventilation system for safety and efficient movement of people and material. This method is risky. Poisonous gases, fires, floods and caving in lead to fatal accidents. Have you ever read about mine fires and flooding of coal mines in India ? The developed economies are retreating from mining, processing and refining stages of production due to high labour costs, while the developing countries with large labour force and striving for higher standard of living are becoming more important. Several countries of Africa and few of South America and Asia have over fifty percent of the earnings from minerals alone. (19.1) Explain the main difference between surface and underground mining. (19.2) Why is open-cast mining the easiest way of mining ? (19.3) Why is shaft mining more risky ?

answer.text:
19.1 Surface mining is cheapest while underground mining is costly; surface mining is practised when the mineral is found close to the surface while underground mining is practised when it is found deep below the surface; surface mining is safe while underground mining is risky; surface mining is called open-cast or strip mining, whereas underground mining is called shaft mining. (Any one point)
19.2 Open-cast mining is the easiest way of mining because it occurs close to the surface.
19.3 Shaft mining is more risky because it is underground mining; therefore poisonous gases, fires, floods and caving in lead to fatal accidents.

questions.text: (a) “Industries maximise profits by reducing costs.” Explain the statement with examples.

answer.text: (a) Industries maximise profits by reducing costs, with examples: (i) Access to market - market means people who have a demand for goods and also have the purchasing power to purchase them; the developed regions of Europe, North America, Japan and Australia provide large global markets as the purchasing power of people is very high. (ii) Access to raw material - raw material used by industries should be cheap and easy to transport; industries based on cheap, bulky and weight-losing material are located close to the sources of raw material, such as steel, sugar and cement industries. (iii) Access to labour supply - some types of manufacturing still require skilled labour; increasing mechanisation, automation and flexibility of industrial processes have reduced the dependence of industries on labour. (iv) Access to sources of energy - industries which use more power are located close to the source of energy supply, such as the aluminium industry. (v) Access to transportation and communication facilities - speedy and efficient transport facilities to carry raw materials to the factory and move finished goods to the market are essential for the development of industries; Western Europe and eastern North America have a highly developed transport system which has always induced the concentration of industries in these areas. (vi) Government policy - governments adopt 'regional policies' to promote balanced economic development and hence set up industries in particular areas. (vii) Access to agglomeration economies. (any five points, or any other relevant point)

questions.text: (b) Explain the classification of industries on the basis of raw materials with examples.

answer.text: (b) Classification of industries on the basis of raw materials, with examples: (i) Agro-based industries - involve the processing of raw materials from the field and the farm into finished products for rural and urban markets, e.g. sugar, pickles, spices, rubber. (ii) Mineral-based industries - use minerals as raw material; some use ferrous metallic minerals like iron and steel industries, and some use non-ferrous metallic minerals like copper and aluminium industries. (iii) Chemical-based industries - use natural chemical minerals, e.g. mineral oil used in the petrochemical industry; salts, sulphur and potash industries also use natural minerals. (iv) Forest-based industries - forests provide many major and minor products used as raw material, e.g. timber for the furniture industry, wood, bamboo and grass for the paper industry. (v) Animal-based industries - leather for the leather industry and wool for woollen textiles are obtained from animals. (any five points, or any other relevant point)

questions.text: (a) Explain the main reasons for uneven distribution of modern manufacturing industries in the world.

answer.text: (a) Main reasons for the uneven distribution of modern manufacturing industries in the world: (i) Access to market - the existence of a market for manufactured goods is the most important factor in the location of industries; remote areas inhabited by few people offer small markets, while the densely populated regions of South and South-East Asia provide large markets. (ii) Access to raw material - raw material used by industries should be cheap and easy to transport; industries based on cheap, bulky and weight-losing material (ores) are located close to the sources of raw material; perishability is a vital factor for the industry to be located closer to the source of raw material. (iii) Access to labour supply - some types of manufacturing still require skilled labour; increasing mechanisation, automation and flexibility of industrial processes have reduced the dependence of industry on labour. (iv) Access to sources of energy - industries which use more power are located close to the source of energy. (v) Access to transportation and communication facilities - speedy and efficient transport facilities to carry raw materials to the factory and move finished goods to the market are essential; improvements in transportation and communication are also important for the exchange and management of information. (vi) Government policy - governments adopt 'regional policies' to promote balanced economic development and set up industries in particular areas. (vii) Access to agglomeration economies/links between industries - many industries benefit from nearness to a leader industry and other industries. (any three points, or any other relevant point)

questions.text: (b) Classify the industries based on product and explain their characteristics.

Consumer goods industries - produce goods consumed by consumers directly, e.g. industries producing bread etc. (any two points to be explained, or any other relevant point)

questions.text: Read the given passage carefully and answer the questions that follow : Tertiary Sector -- When you fall ill you go to your family doctor or you call a doctor. Sometimes your parents take you to a hospital for treatment. While in school, you are taught by your teachers. In the event of any dispute, legal opinion is obtained from a lawyer. Likewise, there are many professionals who provide their services against payment of their fee. Thus, all types of services are special skills provided in exchange of payments. Health, education, law, governance and recreation etc. require professional skills. These services require other theoretical knowledge and practical training. Tertiary activities are related to the service sector. Manpower is an important component of the service sector as most of the tertiary activities are performed by skilled labour, professionally trained experts and consultants. In the initial stages of economic development, larger proportion of people worked in the primary sector. In a developed economy, the majority of workers get employment in tertiary activity and a moderate proportion is employed in the secondary sector. (18.1) Why is ‘manpower’ an important factor of service sector ? Explain. (18.2) Explain the difference between the activities of secondary and tertiary sectors. (18.3) “Tertiary activities include both production and exchange.” Support the statement.

answer.text: (18.1) Manpower is an important factor of the service sector because most of the tertiary activities are performed by skilled labours, professionally trained experts and consultants. (18.2) Difference between the activities of secondary and tertiary sectors: tertiary activities are related to service sectors like transport, banking, etc., whereas secondary activities are related to manufacturing sectors like the cotton textile industry. (18.3) “Tertiary activities include both production and exchange”: the production involves the provision of services that are consumed — the output is indirectly measured in terms of wages and salaries; exchange involves trade, transport and communication facilities.

questions.text: (a) Assess the growth and significance of service sector in the development of the world economy.

answer.text: (a) Growth and significance of the service sector in the world economy: (i) Tertiary activities are related to the service sector. (ii) Manpower is an important component of the service sector as most tertiary activities are performed by skilled labour, professionals, trained experts and consultants. (iii) In a developed economy, the majority of workers are employed in tertiary activities. (iv) Tertiary activities involve the commercial output of services rather than production of tangible goods. (v) Services occur at different levels - some are geared to industry, some to people, some to both, e.g. transport system. (vi) Examples - plumbers, doctors, teachers, lawyers, etc. (vii) State and union legislation have established corporations to supervise and control the marketing of such services, e.g. transport, telecommunication, energy, water supply. (viii) Personal services are available to facilitate people's work, e.g. the Dabbawala service in Mumbai. (any five points, or any other relevant point)

questions.text: “Tertiary activities include both production and exchange.” Explain the statement.

answer.text: Tertiary activities include both production and exchange: (i) The production in tertiary activities includes the provision of services that are consumed. (ii) The output is indirectly measured in terms of wages and salaries. (iii) Exchange involves trade, transport and communication facilities that are used to overcome distance; tertiary activities therefore involve the commercial output of services rather than the production of tangible goods. (iv) They are not directly involved in the processing of physical raw materials. (v) The expertise provided by services relies more heavily on specialised skills, experience and knowledge of the workers rather than on production techniques, machinery and factory processes. (any three points, or any other relevant point)

questions.text: Define the term ‘international trade’. Describe two types of ‘international trade’ in the world.

answer.text: International trade is the exchange of goods and services among countries across national boundaries. Types of international trade in the world: Bilateral trade - done by two countries with each other; they enter into agreement to trade specified commodities amongst them, e.g. country A may agree to trade some raw material with agreement to purchase some specified item from country B or vice versa. Multi-lateral trade - conducted with many trading countries; the same country can trade with a number of other countries; the country may also grant the status of the Most Favoured Nation (MFN) to some of its trading partners.

questions.text: Analyse the five basis of international trade in the world.

answer.text: Basis of international trade in the world: difference in national resources - geological structure, mineral resources, climate; population factors - cultural, size of population; stage of economic development; extent of foreign investment; transport. (Any five points to be analyzed)

questions.text: (a) Explain balance of trade with examples and examine the role of World Trade Organisation (WTO) in international trade.

answer.text:
Balance of Trade: balance of trade records the volume of goods and services imported as well as exported by a country to other countries; if the value of imports is more than the value of a country's exports, the country has a negative or unfavourable balance of trade; if the value of exports is more than the value of imports then the country has a positive or favourable balance of trade. (To be examined as a whole)
Role of World Trade Organisation (WTO) in international trade: it ensures free and fair trade amongst the member nations; it sets the rules for global trading system; it resolves the disputes between the member nations; it also covers trade in services like telecommunication and banking, etc.; it also deals with the issues like intellectual rights. (To be examined by giving any three points)

questions.text: (b) Examine any five bases of international trade.

answer.text: (b) Difference in natural resources like difference in geology, relief, soil and climate; population factor like cultural factors and size of population; stage of economic development; extent/level of foreign investment; means of transport. (To be examined by giving any five points)

questions.text: Explain how geological structures, mineral resources and climate are the bases of international trade.

answer.text: Availability of mineral resources provides the basis for international trade because minerals are unevenly distributed all over the world; lack of adequate transport restricts trade, and efficient means of transport promotes trade by helping in carrying goods from one place to another; climate influences flora and fauna, and also ensures diversity in the range of various products. questions.text: (a) How do differences in national resources become the basis of international trade ? Explain with examples.

answer.text: (a) How differences in national resources become the basis of international trade: the World's national resources are unevenly distributed because of differences in their physical make up i.e. geology, relief, soil and climate. (i) Geological structure: determines the mineral resource base, and topographical differences ensure diversity of crops and animals raised — lowlands have greater agricultural potential, mountains attract tourists and promote tourism. (ii) Mineral resources: they are unevenly distributed the world over — the availability of mineral resources provides the basis for industrial development. (iii) Climate: it influences the type of flora and fauna that can survive in a given region, and ensures diversity in the range of various products — e.g. wool production can take place in cold regions, bananas, rubber and cocoa can grow in tropical regions.

questions.text: (b) Explain the differences between the inland and out-ports with examples.

answer.text: (b) Differences between inland and out ports with examples: (i) Inland Ports — these ports are located away from the sea coast; they are linked to the sea through a river or a canal; ports are accessible to flat bottom ships or barges; for example, Manchester is linked with a canal, Memphis is located on the river Mississippi, Rhine has several ports like Mannheim and Duisburg, and Kolkata is located on the river Hoogli, a branch of the river Ganga. (ii) Out Ports — these are deep water ports built away from the actual ports; these serve the parent ports by receiving those ships which are unable to approach them due to their large size; classic combination, for example, is Athens and its out port Piraeus in Greece.

questions.text: Read the case study given below and answer Q. No. 15 to 17. Ramesh has been working in contract as a welder on a construction site in Talcher (coal region of Odisha) for the last two years. He moved with the contractor to various places like Surat, Mumbai, Gandhi Nagar, Bharuch, Jamnagar and so on. He remits ₹ 20,000 per year to his father in his native village. The remittances have been mainly used for daily consumption, healthcare, schooling of children, etc. Part of the money is also used in agriculture, purchasing of land and building of houses, etc. The standard of living of Ramesh’s family improved significantly. Fifteen years ago, the situation was not the same. The family was passing through very tough times. Three of his brothers and their families had to survive on three acres of land. The family was highly in debt. Ramesh had to discontinue his studies after ninth standard. He was further hard pressed when he got married. Simultaneously, he was also impressed by some successful out-migrants of his village who had been working in Ludhiana and supporting their families in the village by sending money and some consumer goods. Thus, due to abject poverty in the family and perceived job promises at Ludhiana, he made a move to Punjab with his friend. He worked there in a woolen factory for six months at the rate of only ₹ 20 per day in 1988. Apart from the crisis of managing his personal expenditure from this meagre income, he was also facing difficulty in assimilation to the new culture and environment. Then he decided to change his place of work from Ludhiana to Surat under the guidance of his friend. He learnt the skills of welding in Surat and after that he has been moving to different places with the same contractor. Though the economic condition of Ramesh’s family at the village improved, he is bearing the pain of separation of his near and dear ones. He cannot shift them with him, as the job is temporary and transferable. Which one of the following is the meaning of remittance ?

answer.text: Money sent by migrants

questions.chapter: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition
questions.text: (a) Analyse the rural-urban characteristics of Indian population.

answer.text: (a) Rural-urban characteristics of the Indian population: (i) The composition of population by respective places of residence is an important indicator of social and economic characteristics. (ii) This becomes even more significant as about 70% of India's total population lives in villages. (iii) India has a large number of villages and most of them are inhabited. (iv) The rural population distribution is highly uneven. (v) States like Himachal Pradesh and Bihar have a very high percentage of rural population; Goa and Mizoram have only a little over half of their total population residing in villages. (vi) Most UTs have a smaller proportion of rural population, except Dadra and Nagar Haveli (54%). (vii) The proportion of urban population (31.16%) in India is low but growing at a much faster rate over the decades. (viii) The growth rate of urban population has accelerated due to enhanced economic development and improvement in health and hygienic conditions. (ix) The distribution of urban population has a wide variation throughout India. (any five points, or any other relevant point)

questions.chapter: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition
questions.text: (b) Analyse the main features of the composition of working population in India.
questions.topic: Population Composition: Rural-Urban and Occupational Structure

answer.text: (b) Main features of the composition of the working population in India: (i) According to economic status, the population of India is divided into three groups - main workers, marginal workers, and non-workers. (ii) The proportion of workers (both main and marginal) is only 40%. (iii) A vast majority of about 60% are non-workers. (iv) This indicates an economic status with a larger proportion of dependent population, further indicating the possible existence of a large number of unemployed or under-employed people. (v) The occupational composition shows a large proportion of primary sector workers as compared to secondary and tertiary sectors. (vi) The proportion of working population ranges from 29.1% in Lakshadweep (UT) to about 51.9% in Himachal Pradesh (state). (vii) States and UTs with larger percentages of workers are Himachal Pradesh, Sikkim, Chhattisgarh, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur, Meghalaya, and UTs like Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu. (viii) The number of female workers is relatively high in the primary sector. (ix) Male workers outnumber female workers in all sectors. (any five points, or any other relevant point)

questions.chapter: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition
questions.text: (a) “Spatial variation in population density is found in India.” Explain the statement with examples.

answer.text: (a) Spatial variation in population density in India, with examples: (i) Density of population is expressed as the number of persons per unit area. (ii) There is a wide range of spatial variation in population density in the country, ranging from as low as 17 persons per square kilometre in Arunachal Pradesh to 11,297 persons in the National Capital Territory of Delhi. (iii) Among the northern Indian states, Bihar, West Bengal and Uttar Pradesh have higher densities. (iv) Among the peninsular Indian states, Kerala and Tamil Nadu have higher densities. (v) States having moderate densities are Assam, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Haryana, Jharkhand and Odisha. (vi) The hill states of the Himalayan region and north-eastern states (excluding Assam) have relatively low densities, while the union territories (excluding Andaman and Nicobar Islands) have very high densities of population. (any five points, or any other relevant point)

questions.chapter: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition
questions.text: (b) “Population distribution pattern in India is highly uneven.” Explain the statement with examples.

answer.text: (b) The population distribution pattern in India is highly uneven, with examples: (i) Uttar Pradesh has the highest percentage share of population among the states and UTs in the country. (ii) Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Bihar, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Karnataka and Gujarat together account for about 76% of the total population of the country. (iii) The share of population is very small in states like Jammu & Kashmir, Arunachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, despite these states having fairly large geographical areas. (iv) There is a close relationship between population and physical, socio-economic and historical factors. (v) Northern Indian plains, deltas and coastal plains have a higher proportion of population. (vi) Interior districts of southern and central states, the Himalayas, and some north-eastern and western states have lower densities. (any five points, or any other relevant point)

questions.chapter: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition
questions.text: (a) Analyse the regional variation in population growth in India.

answer.text: (a) Regional variation in population growth in India: (i) states like Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and Goa show a low rate of growth. (ii) Kerala registered the lowest growth rate in the country. (iii) a continuous belt of states from west to east in the north-west, north and north-central parts of the country has a relatively high growth rate compared to the southern states. (iv) during 2001 to 2011, the growth rates of almost all states and union territories were low compared to 1991-2001. (v) the percentage decadal growth rates of the six most populous states - Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Bihar, West Bengal, Andhra Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh - all fell during 2001 to 2011 compared to 1991-2001; the fall was lowest for Andhra Pradesh and highest for Maharashtra. (vi) Tamil Nadu and Puducherry registered an increase during 2001-2011 over the previous decade. (any five points, or any other relevant point)

questions.topic: Population Composition: Rural-Urban and Occupational Structure

questions.text: (a) “Urban centres in India are more differentiated in terms of the socio-economic, politico-cultural and other indicators of development.” Evaluate the statement with examples.

answer.text: (a) Urban centres in India are more differentiated in terms of socio-economic, politico-cultural and other indicators of development - evaluated with examples: (i) in urban areas there are farmhouses and high income group localities characterised by well-developed urban infrastructure like wide roads, streetlights, water and sanitation facilities, lawns, well-developed green belts, parks, playgrounds and provisions for individual security and right to privacy. (ii) at the other extreme are slums, jhuggi-jhopari clusters and colonies of shanty structures. (iii) inhabited by people forced to migrate from rural areas in search of livelihood but who could not afford proper housing and landed up living in slums - residential areas of least choice, dilapidated houses, poor hygienic conditions, poor ventilation, lack of basic amenities like drinking water, light and toilet facilities etc. (iv) open defecation, unregulated drainage systems, overcrowded narrow street patterns are serious health and socio-environmental hazards. (v) the slum population works in low-paid, high-risk-prone, unorganised sectors of the urban economy; consequently they are undernourished, prone to different types of diseases and illness, and cannot afford to give proper education to their children. (vi) poverty makes them vulnerable to drug abuse, alcoholism, crime, vandalism, escapism, apathy and ultimately social exclusion. (any five points, or any other relevant point)

questions.text: (b) Explain the evolution of towns in India.

answer.text: (b) Evolution of towns in India (any three points): in India, towns have flourished since prehistoric times like Harappa and Mohenjodaro; India witnessed evolution of towns with many ups and downs until the arrival of Europeans; on the basis of their evolution, Indian towns are classified as (a) Ancient Towns - having a historical background spanning over 2000 years, developed as religious/cultural centres e.g. Varanasi, Prayag (Allahabad), Pataliputra (Patna), Madurai; (b) Medieval Towns - rooted in the medieval period, developed as fort towns on the ruins of ancient towns as headquarters of principalities and kingdoms e.g. Delhi, Hyderabad, Jaipur, Lucknow, Agra, Nagpur; (c) Modern Towns - developed by the British and other Europeans such as Surat, Daman, Goa, Pondicherry; the British later consolidated their hold around Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata, and built hill towns, industrial towns and administrative towns; after independence many towns developed as administrative headquarters - Delhi, Chandigarh, Gandhinagar, Dispur; many industrial towns developed like Durgapur, Bhilai; some old towns developed as satellite towns like Ghaziabad, Rohtak, Gurugram around Delhi.

questions.text: (b) “The land degradation due to man-made processes has greater concern than natural processes.” Evaluate the statement with examples.

answer.text: (b) Land degradation due to man-made processes has greater concern than natural processes - evaluated with examples: (i) faulty strategy of irrigation and agricultural development leads to degradation of land resources, which is serious because it may lead to depletion of soil fertility. (ii) large tracts of agricultural land have lost fertility due to alkalisation and salinisation of soils and waterlogging. (iii) excessive use of chemicals such as insecticides and pesticides has led to their concentration in toxic amounts in the soil profile. (iv) leguminous crops have been displaced from the cropping pattern in irrigated areas, and the duration of fallow has substantially reduced owing to multiple cropping. (v) rainfed areas in humid and semi-arid tropics also experience degradation of several types, like soil erosion by water and wind, often induced by human activities. (vi) wastelands include degraded shifting cultivation areas, degraded land under plantation crops, degraded forests, degraded pastures. (vii) large-scale cutting of trees for agriculture, urbanisation and industries leads to soil erosion, loss of fertility and desertification. (viii) excessive grazing by livestock depletes vegetation cover, leading to soil compaction, erosion and desertification. (ix) mining depletes natural resources, contaminates soil and causes land subsidence. (x) excessive groundwater extraction leads to salinisation and land degradation. questions.text: Read the given passage carefully and answer the questions that follow : Land Degradation -- The pressure on agricultural land increases not only due to the limited availability but also by deterioration of quality of agricultural land. Soil erosion, waterlogging, salinisation and alkalinisation of land lead to land degradation. What happens if land is consistently used without managing its fertility ? Land is degraded and productivity declines. Land degradation is generally understood either as a temporary or a permanent decline in productive capacity of the land. Though all degraded land may not be wasteland, but unchecked process of degradation may lead to the conversion to wasteland. There are two processes that induce land degradation. These are natural and created by human beings. National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC) has classified wastelands by using remote sensing techniques and it is possible to categorise these wastelands according to the processes that have created them. There are a few types of wastelands such as gullied/ravinous land, desertic or coastal sands, barren rocky areas, steep sloping land, and glacial areas, which are primarily caused by natural agents. There are other types of degraded lands such as waterlogged and marshy areas, land affected by salinity and alkalinity and land with or without scrub, which have largely been caused by natural as well as human factors. There are some other types of wastelands such as degraded shifting cultivation area, degraded land under plantation crops, degraded forests, degraded pastures, and mining and industrial wastelands, that are caused by human action. (18.1) Explain the meaning of ‘land degradation’. (18.2) Explain any one man-made process which is responsible for ‘land degradation’. (18.3) Suggest any two measures to solve the problem of land degradation.

answer.text: (18.1) Land degradation is a temporary or permanent decline in the productive capacity of land. (18.2) Man-made processes responsible for land degradation (any one): shifting agriculture, plantation agriculture, degraded forests, degraded pastures, mining and industrial wasteland. (18.3) Measures to solve the problem of land degradation (any two): prevent waterlogging; change agriculture pattern; prevent over-irrigation; afforestation (any other relevant point).

questions.text: (a) Define the concept of ‘Common Property Resource’. Explain any four characteristics of common property resources in India.

answer.text: (a) Common property resources (CPRs) are owned by the state - they are the community's natural resources, where every member has the right of access and usage. Characteristics: (i) In rural areas, such lands are of particular relevance for the livelihood of landless and marginal farmers and other weaker sections. (ii) These provide fodder for livestock and fuel for households. (iii) These provide minor forest products like fruits, nuts, fibre, medicinal plants etc. (iv) These are important for rural women, as most of the fodder and fuel collection is done by them in rural areas. (v) Examples include community forests, pasture lands, village water bodies etc. (any four points, or any other relevant point)

questions.text: (b) Distinguish between ‘irrigated’ and ‘rainfed agriculture’ in India with examples.
questions.topic: Types of Farming: Sources of Moisture

answer.text: (b) Distinguish between irrigated and rainfed agriculture in India with examples: (i) Based on the main source of moisture for crops, farming can be classified as irrigated and rainfed. (ii) Irrigated farming is of two types - protective and productive. (iii) The objective of protective irrigation is to protect crops from the adverse effects of soil moisture deficiency; the objective of productive irrigation is to provide sufficient soil moisture in the cropping season to achieve high productivity. (iv) Rainfed farming is classified on the basis of adequacy of soil moisture during the cropping season into dryland and wetland farming. (v) Dryland farming is largely confined to regions with annual rainfall less than 75 cm, growing hardy and drought-resistant crops such as ragi, bajra, moong, gram and guar (fodder crops); such regions practise various measures of soil moisture conservation and rainwater harvesting. (vi) In wetland farming, rainfall is more than the soil moisture requirement of plants during the rainy season; such areas grow water-intensive crops such as rice, jute and sugarcane. (any five points of distinction, or any other relevant point)

questions.text: (a) Classify Indian farming practices on the basis of source of moisture and describe them.
questions.topic: Types of Farming: Sources of Moisture

answer.text: (a) Classification of Indian farming practices on the basis of source of moisture: farming is classified as irrigated and rainfed (barani). Characteristics: (i) based on the nature of irrigated farming, it is classified as protective and productive. (ii) protective irrigation protects crops from the adverse effects of soil moisture deficiency, with the strategy of providing soil moisture to the maximum possible area. (iii) productive irrigation provides sufficient soil moisture in the cropping season to achieve high productivity. (iv) on the basis of rainfall, farming is classified as rainfed and dryland farming. (v) dryland farming is confined to areas with annual rainfall less than 75 cm, growing hardy crops such as ragi, bajra etc., and practising various measures of soil moisture conservation and rainwater harvesting. (vi) in wetland farming, rainfall exceeds the soil moisture requirement of plants during the rainy season; such regions may face flood and soil erosion hazards, and grow water-intensive crops such as rice, jute and sugarcane. (any four points, or any other relevant point)

questions.text: (b) Define ‘Common Property Resources’. How do ‘Common Property Resources’ help in providing livelihood to the landless and marginal farmers ? Explain.

answer.text: (b) Common Property Resources (CPRs) are defined as a community's natural resource where every member has a right of access and usage with specified obligations, without anybody having property rights over them. How CPRs help provide livelihood to landless and marginal farmers: (i) CPRs provide fodder for livestock and fuel for households, along with other minor forest products like fruits, nuts, fibre, medicinal plants etc. (ii) in rural areas, landless and marginal farmers and other weaker sections depend on income from their livestock because they have limited access to land. (iii) CPRs are important for women, as most fodder and fuel collection is done by them in rural areas. (iv) activities like gathering and selling forest products or grazing livestock on common lands can significantly contribute to their economic stability. (v) examples are community forests, pasture lands, village water bodies and other public spaces. (any four points, or any other relevant point)

questions.text: (a) Explain the problem of ‘low productivity’ of Indian agriculture. Analyse the role of ‘National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture’ to solve this problem.

answer.text: (a) Problem of low productivity of Indian agriculture (any two points): the yield of crops in the country is low in comparison to the international level; per hectare output of most crops such as rice, wheat, cotton and oil seeds in India is much lower than that of USA, Russia and Japan; labour productivity is low in comparison to the international level; vast rainfed areas in the country, especially in drylands, have low yields. National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture (any three points): it aims to make agriculture more productive, sustainable, remunerative and climate resilient; it promotes location-specific and integrated farming systems; it conserves natural resources through appropriate soil and moisture conservation measures; the government has been promoting schemes such as Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana (PKVY) and Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana (RKVY).

questions.text: (b) Explain the problems of the ‘indebtedness’ of Indian farmers. Analyse the importance of ‘farmer’s portal’ in helping the farmers.

answer.text: (b) Problems of indebtedness of Indian farmers (any two points): the inputs of modern agriculture are very expensive; this resource-intensive approach has become unmanageable for marginal and small farmers as they have very meagre or no savings to invest in agriculture; to tide over these difficulties, most farmers have resorted to availing credit from various institutions and money lenders; crop failures and low returns from agriculture have forced them into the trap of indebtedness. Importance of farmer's portal (any three points): it is a platform for farmers to seek any information related to agriculture; detailed information on farmers' insurance, agriculture storage, crops, extension activities, seeds, pesticides and farm machinery is provided; details of fertilizers, market prices, package and practices, and programmes are provided; welfare schemes are also given; block-level details related to soil fertility, storage, insurance and training are available in an interactive map.

questions.text: (a) Examine the agricultural development in India since independence.

answer.text: (a) Any five points to be examined: after Independence, the immediate goal of the government was to increase food-grain production; India switched over from cash crops to food crops, intensified cropping and increased cultivated area by bringing cultivable and fallow land under plough; agricultural production stagnated during the late 1950s, so the Intensive Agricultural District Programme (IADP) and Intensive Agricultural Area Programme (IAAP) were launched; new high-yielding varieties (HYVs) of wheat (Mexico) and rice (Philippines) became available for cultivation by the mid-1960s; India introduced the package technology comprising HYVs along with chemical fertilizers in irrigated areas of Punjab, Haryana, Western Uttar Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh and Gujarat; this strategy increased food-grain production at a very fast rate, a spurt of growth known as the Green Revolution; it also gave a fillip to the development of agro-input, agro-processing and small-scale industries; the country became self-reliant in food-grain production.

questions.text: (b) Examine the various problems of Indian agriculture.

answer.text: (b) Any five points to be examined: dependence on erratic monsoon - irrigation covers only about 33 per cent of cultivated area, so crop production in the rest of the cultivated land directly depends on rain, and drought is common in low-rainfall areas; low productivity - crop yields are low compared to the international level, and labour productivity is also low due to high pressure on land resources; constraints of financial resources and indebtedness - inputs of modern agriculture are expensive, which has become unmanageable for marginal and small farmers with meagre or no savings; lack of land reforms has resulted in continued inequitable distribution of cultivable land; small farm size and fragmentation of landholdings makes farming uneconomic; lack of commercialisation - many farmers produce for self-consumption, restricting modernisation to irrigated areas; vast underemployment in the agricultural sector, particularly in unirrigated tracts; degradation of cultivable land due to faulty irrigation and agricultural strategies, leading to alkalisation, salinisation and water-logging, and excessive use of chemicals causing toxic concentrations in the soil.

questions.text: Read the case study given below and answer the questions from 15 to 17. Case Study : Indira Gandhi Canal (Nahar) Command Area -- Indira Gandhi Canal, previously known as the Rajasthan Canal, is one of the largest canal systems in India. Conceived by Kanwar Sain in 1948, the canal project was launched on 31 March, 1958. The canal originates at Harike barrage in Punjab and runs parallel to Pakistan border at an average distance of 40 km in Thar Desert (Marusthali) of Rajasthan. The total planned length of the system is 9,060 km catering to the irrigation needs of a total culturable command area of 19{\cdot}63 lakh hectares. Out of the total command area, about 70 percent was envisaged to be irrigated by flow system and the rest by lift system. The construction work of the canal system has been carried out through two stages. The command area of Stage-I lies in Ganganagar, Hanumangarh and northern part of Bikaner districts. It has a gently undulating topography and its culturable command area is 5{\cdot}53 lakh hectares. The command area of Stage-II is spread over Bikaner, Jaisalmer, Barmer, Jodhpur, Nagaur and Churu districts covering culturable command area of 14{\cdot}10 lakh ha. It comprises desert land dotted with shifting sand dunes and temperature soaring to 50°C in summers. In the lift canal, the water is lifted up to make it to flow against the slope of the land. All the lift canals of Indira Gandhi system originate at the left bank of main canal while all the canals on the right bank of main canal are flow channels. Irrigation in Stage-I command area of the canal was introduced in early 1960s, whereas the command area of Stage-II began receiving irrigation in mid-1980s. The introduction of canal irrigation in this dry land has transformed its ecology, economy and society. It has influenced the environmental conditions of the region both positively as well as negatively. The availability of soil moisture for a longer period of time and various afforestation and pasture development programmes under CAD have resulted in greening the land. This has also helped in reducing wind erosion and siltation of canal systems. But the intensive irrigation and excessive use of water has led to the emergence of twin environmental problems of waterlogging and soil salinity. What was the main objective to construct of Indira Gandhi Canal ?
options: Proving water for irrigation in the command area

answer.text: Proving water for irrigation in the command area

questions.text: Explain with examples how watershed management and rainwater harvesting help in conserving water resources in India.

answer.text:
Watershed Management: it is a way of efficient water management; it includes conservation, regeneration and judicious use of all natural and human resources within a watershed area; it involves prevention of runoff; it helps in storage and recharge of groundwater through various methods like recharge wells, percolation tanks, etc. Examples of watershed management: Haryali, Neeru-Meeru and Aryaya Pani Sansad. Rainwater Harvesting: it is an effective method of recharging aquifers; it is a low cost and eco-friendly technique of preserving water; rainwater can be preserved and guided to bore-wells, pits or wells to recharge the underground water; it improves the quality of groundwater, increases the groundwater table, prevents flooding and soil erosion and arrests the salt water intrusion in the coastal areas. Examples of rainwater harvesting: service wells, recharge wells, tanka/kund, check dams, rooftop rainwater harvesting, etc. (To be examined as a whole)

(iii) Spread of canal irrigation has led to increase in cultivated area and crop intensity. (iv) Traditional crops of jowar, bajra has been replaced by rice and wheat etc.

answer.text: (ii), (iii) and (iv) only are correct.

questions.text: Suggest the measures to achieve the objectives of ‘Namami Gange Programme’.

answer.text: Measures to achieve the objectives of the 'Namami Gange Programme': (i) Developing sewerage treatment systems in towns. (ii) Monitoring of industrial effluents. (iii) Development of river front. (iv) Afforestation along the banks for increased biodiversity. (v) Cleaning of the river surface. (vi) Development of 'Ganga Grams' in Uttarakhand, UP, Bihar, Jharkhand and West Bengal. (vii) Creating public awareness to avoid adding pollutants into the river even in the form of rituals. (any three points, or any other relevant point)

questions.text: (a) “India’s water demand is highly dominated by irrigational needs.” Evaluate the statement.

answer.text: (a) India's water demand is highly dominated by irrigational needs: (i) In agriculture, water is mainly used for irrigation, as irrigation is needed due to the spatio-temporal variability of rainfall in the country. (ii) Large tracts of the country are deficient in rainfall and are drought prone - for example, north-western India and the Deccan Plateau. (iii) Winter and summer seasons are more or less dry in most parts of the country. (iv) It is difficult to practise agriculture without assured irrigation during dry seasons. (v) In areas of ample rainfall, breaks in the monsoon or its failure creates dry spells detrimental for agriculture. (vi) Certain crops like rice and sugarcane (high yielding varieties) need regular moisture supply, made possible only by a developed irrigational system. (vii) Irrigation makes multiple cropping possible. (viii) Irrigated lands have higher agricultural productivity than unirrigated lands. (any five points, or any other relevant point)

questions.text: (b) “In India, water resources are getting polluted with industrial effluents, domestic waste and insecticides used in agriculture.” Evaluate the statement.

answer.text: (b) Water resources getting polluted with industrial effluents, domestic waste and insecticides: (i) Available water resources are getting polluted with industrial, agricultural and domestic effluents. (ii) It is limiting the availability of usable water resources. (iii) Water gets polluted by foreign matters such as micro-organisms, chemicals, industrial and other wastes. (iv) Drains carrying agricultural (fertilizers and insecticides), domestic (solid and liquid wastes) and industrial effluents join the rivers. (v) The concentration of pollutants in rivers remains very high during the summer season. (vi) Toxic substances entering different water bodies get dissolved or lie suspended in water. (vii) As a result, the quality of water deteriorates, affecting aquatic systems. (viii) Whenever these pollutants seep down, they pollute groundwater. (any five points, or any other relevant point)

questions.text: Choose the correct group of states utilizing their groundwater resource moderately.

answer.text: Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar

questions.text: Choose an objective of the ‘Namami Gange Programme’ from the following :
options: To develop the network of canals
To construct dams for water management

answer.text: To monitor industrial effluents

questions.text: (a) Explain the main objectives of ‘Jal Kranti Abhiyan’ in India.
questions.topic: Jal Kranti Abhiyan and National Water Policy

answer.text: (a) Main objectives of the 'Jal Kranti Abhiyan' in India: (i) to ensure water security through per capita availability of water in the country. (ii) it aims at involving local bodies, NGOs and citizens at large in creating awareness regarding its objectives. (iii) to provide livelihood and food security through water security. (iv) many activities have been proposed under Jal Kranti Abhiyan, like selection of one water-stressed village to create a 'Jal Gram'. (v) water conservation and artificial recharge. (vi) reducing groundwater pollution. (vii) construction of arsenic-free wells in selected areas. (viii) identification of model command areas in different parts of the country. (any five points, or any other relevant point)

questions.text: (b) Explain the different methods of rainwater harvesting in India.

answer.text: (b) Different methods of rainwater harvesting in India: (i) traditional rainwater harvesting methods include surface storage bodies like lakes, ponds etc. (ii) depending on the region, different methods have been practised in the country, like the 'tanka' in Rajasthan. (iii) roof-top rainwater harvesting. (iv) surface runoff harvesting. (v) recharge wells harvesting. (vi) community participation and awareness. (vii) watershed development. (viii) harvesting through service wells. (any five points, or any other relevant point)
