questions.text: (a) “The intensive irrigation in the areas of successful ‘green revolution’ have both positive and negative impacts.” Analyse the statement.

answer.text: (a) Positive impacts (any three): provision of irrigation makes multiple cropping possible; irrigated lands have higher agricultural productivity than unirrigated lands; HYV crops need a regular moisture supply, made possible only by a developed irrigation system; wheat and rice are grown mainly with the help of irrigation in states like Punjab, Haryana and Western Uttar Pradesh. Negative impacts (any two): over-use of ground water resources in Punjab, Haryana and Western Uttar Pradesh has led to a decline in ground water, which will impact food production; salinity and alkalinity are increasing in the soil, which negatively affects crop growth; in some parts, accumulation of arsenic is taking place. (If a student writes three negative and two positive points instead, that should also be considered.)

questions.text: (b) “The groundwater utilization is very high in the states where ‘green revolution’ is successful.” Analyse the statement.

answer.text: (b) Any five points to be analysed: the Green Revolution strategy of agricultural development has largely been successful in Punjab, Haryana and Western Uttar Pradesh due to a developed irrigation system; in Punjab, Haryana and Western Uttar Pradesh, more than 85% of the net sown area is under irrigation; of the total net irrigated area, 76.1% in Punjab is irrigated through wells and tube wells; in Haryana, 51.3% of the net irrigated area is irrigated through wells and tube wells; HYV crops need a regular moisture supply, made possible only by a developed irrigation system mainly through wells and tube wells; over-use of ground water resources has led to a decline in the ground water table in the states of Punjab and Haryana.

topic_order: Jal Kranti Abhiyan and National Water Policy

questions.text: (a) Mention the main characteristics of the mineral belt of ‘South-Western Plateau Region’ of India.
questions.topic: Distribution of Minerals: The Mineral Belts

answer.text: (a) Characteristics of the mineral belt of the South-Western Plateau region of India: this belt extends over Karnataka, Goa, and contiguous Tamil Nadu uplands and Kerala; this belt is rich in ferrous metals and bauxite; it also contains high grade iron ore, manganese and limestone; this belt lacks coal deposits except the Neyveli lignite mines. (Any three points to be mentioned)

questions.text: (b) Mention the main characteristics of mineral belt of ‘North-Western Region’ of India.
questions.topic: Distribution of Minerals: The Mineral Belts

answer.text: (b) Characteristics of the mineral belt of the North-Western region of India: this belt extends along the Aravali in Rajasthan and part of Gujarat; minerals are associated with the Dharwar system of rocks; copper and zinc have been the major minerals; Rajasthan is rich in building stones, i.e. sandstone, granite, marble etc. (Any three points to be mentioned)

questions.text: (a) Describe coal as source of conventional energy in India.

answer.text: (a) Coal as a source of conventional energy in India: it is an exhaustible resource; coal is one of the important minerals mainly used in the generation of thermal power; coal is also used in smelting of iron ore; about 80% of the coal deposits in India is of bituminous type; the most important Gondwana coal fields of India are located in the Damodar Valley. (Any three points to be explained)

questions.text: (b) Describe the importance of solar energy as a source of non-conventional energy in India.

answer.text: (b) Importance of solar energy as a source of non-conventional energy in India: sun rays tapped in photovoltaic cells can be converted into energy, known as solar energy; solar thermal technology has some relative advantages over all other non-renewable energy sources; it is cost competitive; it is environment friendly; it is easy to construct; it is generally used in appliances like solar heaters, crop dryers, cookers etc. (Any three points to be explained)

questions.text: “Most of the metallic minerals in India occur in the peninsular plateau region in the old crystalline rocks.” Examine the statement.
questions.topic: Distribution of Minerals: The Mineral Belts

answer.text: Most of the metallic minerals in India occur in the peninsular plateau region in the old crystalline rocks: our Peninsular plateau is rich in mineral resources; metallic minerals occur in igneous rocks and the plateau has largely igneous rocks; the Chhota Nagpur region in Jharkhand, Odisha and West Bengal is rich in iron ore, manganese, bauxite and mica; Karnataka, Goa and Tamil Nadu are rich in iron ore and manganese, Goa has large iron ore deposits; the Gujarat-Rajasthan belt consists of copper, zinc, sandstone, granite and gypsum. (Any five points to be examined)

questions.text: “Petroleum is an essential source of energy for running transport and industry.” Examine the statement.

answer.text: Petroleum is an essential source of energy for all types of internal combustion engines; today automobiles, railways and airways are highly dependent on petroleum; it is used as raw material in many industries; the petroleum by-products provide the raw material for many industries like synthetic fibre, medicines, fertilizers, rubber, Vaseline, etc. (To be examined by giving any three points)

questions.text: (a) Analyze the relationship between the conservation of mineral resources and sustainable development in India.

answer.text: (a) Relationship between conservation of mineral resources and sustainable development: the challenge of sustainable development requires integrating the quest for economic development with environmental concerns; traditional methods of resource use generate enormous quantities of waste and create other environmental problems; sustainable development calls for protection of resources for future generations, so there is an urgent need to conserve resources; alternative energy sources like solar, wind, wave and geothermal energy are inexhaustible and should be developed to replace exhaustible resources; for metallic minerals, use of scrap metal enables recycling, especially significant for metals like copper, lead and zinc; use of substitutes for scarce metals may reduce their consumption; export of strategic and scarce minerals must be reduced (any five points to be analysed).

questions.text: (b) Analyze the advantages of non-conventional energy sources by giving the example of solar energy in India.

answer.text: (b) Advantages of non-conventional energy sources: inexhaustible resources which are abundantly available; more equitably distributed; environment-friendly; renewable energy sources like solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, biomass, etc.; more sustained and eco-friendly; cheaper energy sources; full potential to replace conventional sources of energy. Solar energy example: cost-competitive; environment-friendly; easy to construct; used more in appliances like heaters, crop dryers, coolers, etc.; the western part of India like Gujarat and Rajasthan has greater potential (any five points to be analysed).

questions.text: Choose the correct option to fill in the blank in the flow chart : Minerals → Metallic / Non-metallic; Non-metallic → Fuel mineral (Example – Coal) / Other non-metallic minerals (Example ______)

answer.text: Graphite

questions.text: “Nuclear power has emerged as a viable source in recent years.” Examine the statement with suitable arguments in the context of India.

answer.text: Nuclear power in the context of India: important minerals used for generating nuclear energy are uranium and thorium — uranium deposits occur in the Dharwar rocks; geographically, uranium ores are known to occur at several locations along the Singhbhum Copper belt; thorium is mainly obtained from monazite and ilmenite in the beach sands along the coast of Kerala and Tamil Nadu; the world's richest monazite deposits occur in Palakkad and Kollam; the Atomic Energy Commission was established in 1948, but progress could be made only after the establishment of the Atomic Energy Institute at Trombay in 1954, later renamed the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre; important nuclear power projects are Tarapur, Rawatbhata, Kalpakkam, Narora, Kaiga and Kakrapara (any five points to be explained).

questions.text: (a) Explain any five measures for the conservation of mineral resources in India.

answer.text: (a) Any five measures for the conservation of mineral resources in India: sustainable development calls for the protection of resources for future generations; there is an urgent need to conserve energy sources like solar power, wind etc. which are inexhaustible resources; in case of metallic minerals, use of scrap metals will enable recycling of metals — use of scrap is especially significant in metals like copper, lead and zinc in which India's reserves are meagre; use of substitutes for scarce metals may also reduce their consumption; export of strategic and scarce minerals must be reduced; substitutes should be developed to replace exhaustible resources.

questions.text: (b) Explain the importance of solar energy in Indian context.

answer.text: (b) Importance of solar energy in the Indian context: sun rays tapped in photovoltaic cells can be converted into energy, known as solar energy; solar thermal technology has some relative advantages over all other non-renewable energy sources; it is cost competitive, environment friendly and easy to construct; solar energy is 7 per cent more effective than coal or oil based plants and 10 per cent more effective than nuclear plants; it is generally used more in appliances like heaters, crop dryers, cookers, etc.

questions.text: Why should non-conventional sources of energy be used in India for sustainable development ? Explain with examples.

answer.text: Non-conventional sources of energy should be used in India for sustainable development: (i) Sustainable development requires integration of the quest for economic development with environmental concerns. (ii) Traditional methods of resource use generate enormous quantities of waste and create other environmental problems like pollution. (iii) It calls for protection of resources for future generations. (iv) Alternative sources of energy like solar power, wind, wave and geo-thermal energy are inexhaustible. (v) Non-conventional sources of energy are more cost-effective than conventional sources, particularly petroleum, as the import cost of petroleum is higher. (any three points, or any other relevant point)

questions.text: (a) “Petroleum is an essential source of energy and many byproducts are associated with its refining.” Explain this statement with examples.

answer.text: (a) Petroleum as an essential source of energy with by-products from refining: (i) Petroleum is an essential source of energy for all internal combustion engines in automobiles, railways and aircraft. (ii) Petroleum is referred to as liquid gold because of its scarcity and diversified uses. (iii) Crude petroleum consists of hydrocarbons of liquid and gaseous state, varying in chemical composition, colour and specific gravity. (iv) Its numerous by-products are processed in petrochemical industries such as fertilizers, synthetic rubber, synthetic fiber, medicines, Vaseline, lubricants, wax, soap and cosmetics. (v) Petroleum is also used for thermal power production. (any five points, or any other relevant point)

questions.text: (b) “The generation of energy through non-conventional sources is the need of the hour for sustainable development.” Explain the statement with examples.

answer.text: (b) Generation of energy through non-conventional sources for sustainable development: (i) Fossil fuels - coal, petroleum and natural gas - are expensive, exhaustible sources and cause widespread pollution. (ii) Non-conventional sources of energy - solar, wind, biomass, geothermal - provide sustainable energy, are cost-competitive, environment-friendly, non-exhaustible and easy to construct. (iii) Rajasthan and Gujarat have great potential for development of solar energy. (iv) Wind energy is already generated in Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra and Karnataka. (v) In India, a geothermal energy plant has been commissioned at Manikaran in Himachal Pradesh. (vi) Biomass energy is produced by processing waste and garbage to produce electricity. (vii) These alternative sources of energy are inexhaustible and should be developed to replace exhaustible sources. (any five points, or any other relevant point)

questions.text: (a) Explain the significance of petroleum as major source of energy and describe its distribution in India.

answer.text: (a) Significance of petroleum as a major source of energy (any three points): petroleum is an essential source of energy for all internal combustion engines in automobiles, railways and aircraft; it has numerous by-products processed and used in petrochemical industries like fertilizers, synthetic rubber, fibre, medicines, vaseline, lubricants, wax, soap and cosmetics; petroleum is scarce but has diversified uses, so it is referred to as liquid gold; in 1956 the government set up the Oil and Natural Gas Commission (ONGC) for systematic exploration and production of oil and natural gas. Distribution of petroleum in India (any two points): Digboi, Naharkatiya and Moran in Assam; Ankaleshwar, Kalol, Mehsana, Nawagam, Kosamba and Lunej in Gujarat; Mumbai High in the Arabian Sea; exploratory wells of the Krishna-Godavari and Kaveri basins on the east coast.

questions.text: (b) Explain the significance of iron-ore as industrial raw material and describe its distribution in India.

answer.text: (b) Significance of iron-ore as industrial raw material (any three points): it provides a strong base for the development of metallurgical industries; India is endowed with fairly abundant resources of iron ore and has the largest reserve of iron ore in Asia; the two main types of iron ore found in India are hematite and magnetite; it has great demand in the international market due to its superior quality; iron ore mines occur in close proximity to coal fields in the north-eastern plateau region, which adds to its advantage. Distribution of iron ore in India (any two points): Odisha is the leading producer, with iron ore occurring in a series of hill ranges in Sundergarh, Mayurbhanj and Jhar; major regions in Jharkhand are Poorbi and Pashchimi Singhbhum districts; major regions in Chhattisgarh are Durg, Dantewara and Bailadila; major regions in Karnataka are Ballari, Chikkamagaluru, Shivamogga, Chitradurg and Tumakuru; major regions in Maharashtra are Chandrapur, Bhandara and Ratnagiri; major regions in Telangana are Karimnagar and Warangal; major regions in Andhra Pradesh are Kurnool, Cuddapah and Anantapur; major regions in Tamil Nadu are Salem and Nilgiris; Goa has also emerged as an important producer of iron ore.

questions.text: (a) “Non-conventional energy sources are equitably distributed in India.” Justify the statement with suitable arguments.

answer.text: (a) Any five points to be justified: nuclear energy - important minerals used are uranium and thorium; uranium deposits occur in the Dharwar rocks, along the Singbhum Copper belt, and in Udaipur, Alwar and Jhunjhunu districts of Rajasthan, Durg district of Chhattisgarh, Bhandara district of Maharashtra and Kullu district of Himachal Pradesh; thorium is mainly obtained from monazite and ilmenite in beach sands along the coast of Kerala and Tamil Nadu; solar energy - sun rays tapped in photovoltaic cells are converted into energy, and the western part of India (Gujarat and Rajasthan) has greater potential for solar energy development; wind energy - Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra and Karnataka have favourable conditions; tidal and wave energy - India has great potential along the coasts; geothermal energy - a plant has been commissioned at Manikaran in Himachal Pradesh; bio-energy - processes waste and garbage to produce energy, e.g. the Okhla project converting municipal waste into energy in Delhi.

questions.text: (b) “The conventional sources of energy need to be replaced due to their exhaustibility.” Justify the statement with suitable arguments.

answer.text: (b) Any five points to be justified: mineral fuels like coal, petroleum and natural gas (fossil fuels) and nuclear energy minerals are the conventional sources of energy; fossil fuels and nuclear energy use exhaustible raw materials that take millions of years to form; they are depleting at a faster rate due to rapid industrialisation and demand; these energy sources are expensive; the use of conventional sources generates enormous quantities of waste and creates other environmental problems; alternative energy sources like solar, wind, wave and geothermal energy should be used instead.

questions.text: “Attaining sustainable development in the Indira Gandhi Canal (Nahar) Command Area requires major thrust upon the measures to achieve ecological sustainability.” Evaluate the statement.
questions.topic: Case Study: Indira Gandhi Canal Command Area

answer.text: Attaining sustainable development in the Indira Gandhi Canal (Nahar) Command Area requires major thrust on measures to achieve ecological sustainability: strict implementation of water management policy is the first requirement; the canal project envisages protective irrigation in Stage-I and extensive irrigation of crops and pasture development in Stage-II; in general the cropping pattern shall not include water intensive crops, people should be encouraged to grow plantation crops such as citrus fruits; CAD programmes such as lining of water courses, land development and levelling and warabandi system shall be effectively implemented to reduce the conveyance loss of water; areas affected by water-logging and soil salinity shall be reclaimed; eco-development through afforestation, shelter belt plantation and pasture development is necessary particularly in the fragile environment of Stage-II. (Any five points to be explained)

questions.text: Study the following source and answer the Question No. 15 to 17. A Case Study -- Jhabua district is located in the westernmost agro-climatic zone in Madhya Pradesh. It is, in fact, one of the five most backward districts of the country. It is characterized by high concentration of tribal population (mostly Bhils). The people suffer due to poverty which has been accentuated by the high rate of resource degradation, both forest and land. The watershed management programmes funded by both the ministries of “Rural Development” and “Agriculture”, Government of India, have been successfully implemented in Jhabua district which has gone a long way in preventing land degradation and improving soil quality. Watershed Management Programmes acknowledge the linkage between land, water and vegetation and attempts to improve livelihoods of people through natural resource management and community participation. In the past five years, the programmes funded by the Ministry of Rural Development alone (implemented by Rajiv Gandhi Mission for Watershed Management) has treated 20 percent of the total area under Jhabua district. Which among the following is correct meaning of ‘land degradation’ ?
questions.topic: Case Study: Jhabua District — Watershed Management

answer.text: Declining productivity of the land

questions.text: Read the case study given below and answer Q. No. 15 to 17. Case Study -- Integrated Tribal Development Project in Bharmaur Region -- Bharmaur tribal area comprises Bharmaur and Holi tehsils of Chamba district of Himachal Pradesh. It is a notified tribal area since 21st November, 1975. Bharmaur is inhabited by ‘Gaddi’, a tribal community who have maintained a distinct identity in the Himalayan region as they practised transhumance and conversed through Gaddiali dialect. Bharmaur tribal region has harsh climate conditions, low resource base and fragile environment. These factors have influenced the society and economy of the region. According to the 2011 census, the total population of Bharmaur sub-division was 39,113 i.e., 21 persons per sq km. It is one of the most (economically and socially) backward areas of Himachal Pradesh. Historically, the Gaddis have experienced geographical and political isolation and socio-economic deprivation. The economy is largely based on agriculture and allied activities such as sheep and goat rearing. The process of development of tribal area of Bharmaur started in 1970s when Gaddis were included among ‘scheduled tribes’. Under the Fifth Five Year Plan, the tribal sub-plan was introduced in 1974 and Bharmaur was designated as one of the five Integrated Tribal Development Projects (ITDP) in Himachal Pradesh. This area development plan was aimed at improving the quality of life of the Gaddis. Bharmaur Tribal region belongs to which of the following states ?
questions.topic: Integrated Tribal Development Project: Bharmaur Region

answer.text: Himachal Pradesh

questions.text: Read the following source and answer the question no. 15 to 17. A Case Study -- Jhabua district is located in the westernmost agro-climatic zone in Madhya Pradesh. It is, in fact, one of the five most backward districts of the country. It is characterized by high concentration of tribal population (mostly Bhils). The people suffer due to poverty which has been accentuated by the high rate of resource degradation, both forest and land. The watershed management programmes funded by both the Ministries of “Rural Development” and “Agriculture”, Government of India, have been successfully implemented in Jhabua district which has gone a long way in preventing land degradation and improving soil quality. Watershed Management Programmes acknowledge the linkage between land, water and vegetation and attempts to improve livelihoods of people through natural resource management and community participation. In the past five years the programmes funded by the Ministry of Rural Development alone (implemented by Rajiv Gandhi Mission for Watershed Management) has treated 20 percent of the total area under Jhabua district. The Petlawad Development block of Jhabua is located in the northernmost part of the district and represents an interesting and successful case of Government-NGO partnership and community participation in managing watershed programmes. The Bhils in Petlawad Development block, for example, (Sat Rundi hamlet of Karravat village) through their own efforts, have revitalized large parts of common property resources. Each household planted and maintained one tree on the common property. They also have planted fodder grass on the pasture land and adopted social-fencing of these lands for at least two years. Even after that, they say, there would be no open grazing on these lands, but stall feeding of cattle, and they are thus confident that the pastures they have developed would sustain their cattle in future. An interesting aspect of this experience is that before the community embarked upon the process of management of the pasture, there was encroachment on this land by a villager from an adjoining village. The villagers called the tehsildar to ascertain the rights of the common land. The ensuing conflict was tackled by the villagers by offering to make the defaulter encroaching on the CPR a member of their user group and sharing the benefits of greening the common lands / pastures. Why did the people of Jhabua tribal community suffer from poverty ? Choose the option which is NOT correct.

questions.text: Read the given passage carefully and answer the questions that follow : Integrated Tribal Development Project in Bharmaur Region -- This region lies between 32° 11' N and 32° 41' N latitudes and 76° 22' E and 76° 53' E longitudes. Spread over an area of about 1,818 sq km, the region mostly lies between 1,500 m to 3,700 m above the mean sea level. This region popularly known as the homeland of Gaddis is surrounded by lofty mountains on all sides. It has Pir Panjal in the north and Dhaula Dhar in the South. In the east, the extension of Dhula Dhar converges with Pir Panjal near Rohtang Pass. The river Ravi and its tributaries – the Budhil and the Tundahen, drain this territory, and carve out deep gorges. These rivers divide the region into four physiographic divisions called Holi, Khani, Kugti and Tundah areas. Bharmaur experiences freezing weather conditions and snowfall in winter. Its mean monthly temperature in January remains 4°C and in July 26°C. (18.1) Describe the location of Bharmaur region. (18.2) Why does this region experience harsh climatic conditions ? questions.chapter: Planning and Sustainable Development in Indian Context
questions.text: (a) Explain the meaning of ‘target area planning’. Analyse the need of ‘target area planning’ for development.

answer.text: (a) Target Area Planning: The approach to address regional imbalance by focusing on the resource base of the economically backward region is known as target area planning. Need of target area planning for development: (i) The economic development of a region depends upon its resource base; sometimes resource-rich regions remain backward. (ii) To arrest the accentuation of regional and social disparities, the Planning Commission introduced the 'target area' and 'target group' approaches to planning. (iii) It was realized that regional imbalances in economic development were getting accentuated. (iv) Target areas include 'Command Area Development Programme', 'Drought Prone Areas Development Programme', 'Desert Development Programme', etc. (v) In the 8th Five Year Plan, special area programmes were designed to develop infrastructure in hill areas, north-eastern states, tribal areas and backward areas. (any four points, or any other relevant point)

questions.text: Read the given source and answer the questions that follow : The main sources of noise pollution are various factories, mechanized construction and demolition works, automobiles and aircraft, etc. There may be added periodical but polluting noise from sirens, loudspeakers used in various festivals, programmes associated with community activities. The level of steady noise is measured by sound level expressed in terms of decibels (dB). Of all these sources, the biggest nuisance is the noise produced by traffic, because its intensity and nature depend upon factors, such as the type of aircraft, vehicle, train and the condition of road, as well as, that of vehicle (in case of automobiles). In sea traffic, the noise pollution is confined to the harbour due to loading and unloading activities being carried. Industries cause noise pollution but with varying intensity depending upon the type of industry. Noise pollution is location specific and its intensity declines with increase in distance from the source of pollution, i.e. industrial areas, arteries of transportation, airport, etc. Noise pollution is hazardous in many metropolitan and big cities in India. (18.1) Explain the meaning of noise pollution. (18.2) Why is noise pollution hazardous in metropolitan cities in India ? (18.3) “Noise pollution is location specific.” Explain with argument.

answer.text:
18.1 Noise pollution refers to the state of unbearable and uncomfortable conditions to human beings.
18.2 Noise pollution is hazardous in metropolitan cities in India due to industrial areas, arteries of transportation, airports etc.
18.3 Noise pollution is location specific because its intensity declines with increase in distance from the source of pollution.

questions.text: Read the case study given below and answer the questions that follow : Case Study : A Role Model to Restore the Ecology and Safeguard Human Health in Daurala -- Based on the universal law “Polluter pays”, effort to restore the ecology and safeguard the human health with people’s participation has taken place in Daurala near Meerut. These efforts are now bearing fruits after a span of three years when a Meerut based NGO had developed a model for ecological restoration. The meeting of the Daurala industries officials, NGOs, Government officials and other stakeholders at Meerut has brought out results. The powerful logics, authentic studies and the pressure of people have brought a new lease of life to the twelve thousand residents of this village. It was in the year 2003 that the pitiable condition of Dauralaites drew the attention of the civil society. The groundwater of this village was contaminated with heavy metals. The reason was that the untreated wastewater of Daurala industries was leaching to the groundwater table. The NGOs conducted a door-to-door survey of the health status of the residents and came out with a report. The organisation, the village community and people’s representatives sat together to find out sustainable solutions to the health problem. The industrialists showed a keen interest towards checking the deteriorating ecology. The overhead water tank’s capacity in the village was enhanced and a 900 m extra pipeline was laid to supply potable water to the community. The silted pond of the village was cleaned and recharged by desilting it. Large quantity of silt was removed paving way to large quantity of water so that it recharged the aquifers, Rainwater harvesting structures have been constructed at different places which has helped in diluting the contaminants of the groundwater after the monsoon. 1000 trees have also been planted which have improved the environment. (19.1) What is meant by water pollution ? (19.2) Explain the role of industrialists in checking the deteriorating ecology. (19.3) Analyse the contribution of the NGO in Daurala’s problem.

answer.text:
19.1 Water pollution means water gets contaminated with heavy metals.
19.2 Role of industrialists in checking deteriorating ecology: the overhead water tank's capacity was enhanced and 900 m of extra pipeline was laid to supply potable water; the silted pond was cleaned and recharged by desilting.
19.3 Contribution of the NGO in Daurala's problem: the NGO developed a model for ecological restoration and conducted a door-to-door survey of the health status of the residents and came out with a report.

questions.text: Read the given passage carefully and answer the questions that follow : Dharavi -- There is only one main road that traverses Dharavi, which has been reduced to less than half of that for most of its length. Some of the side alleys and lanes are so narrow that not even a bicycle can pass. The whole neighbourhood consists of temporary buildings, two or three storeyed high with rusty iron stairways to the upper part, where a single room is rented by a whole family, sometimes accommodating 10 – 12 people; it is a kind of tropical version of the industrial dwelling of Victorian London’s East End. But Dharavi is a keeper of more sombre secrets than the revulsion it inspires in the rich; a revulsion, moreover, that is, in direct proportion to the role it serves in the creation of the wealth of Bombay. In this place of shadowless, treeless sunlight, uncollected garbage, stagnant pools of foul water, where the only creatures are the shining black crows and long grey rats, some of the of the most beautiful, valuable and useful articles in India are made. From Dharavi come delicate ceramics and pottery, exquisite embroidery and zari work, sophisticated leather goods, high-fashion garments, finely-wrought metalwork, delicate jewellery settings, wood carvings and furniture that would find its way into the houses, both in India and abroad. (18.1) Describe the physical condition of Dharavi. (18.2) Explain one major problem of Dharavi. (18.3) Explain the main objective of ‘Swachh Bharat Mission’ in the context of Dharavi.

answer.text: (18.1) Physical condition of Dharavi (any one): infrastructure is very poor — only one main road traverses the slums, reduced to less than half its length for most of its length; the whole neighbourhood consists of temporary buildings, two or three storeyed high, with rusty iron stairways to the upper part; it is a place of shadowless, treeless sunlight, uncollected garbage, and stagnant pools of foul water. (18.2) One major problem of Dharavi (any one): lack of good living conditions; overcrowded areas; temporary houses. (18.3) Objective of Swachh Bharat Mission in the context of Dharavi: the SBM is part of the urban renewal mission launched by the Govt. of India to improve the quality of life in urban slums.

questions.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
questions.text: (a) Evaluate the impact of urban waste disposal problem and suggest any two measures to overcome it.
questions.topic: Urban Waste Disposal and Solid Waste

answer.text: (a) Impact of urban waste disposal problems and measures to overcome it: (i) Household waste is disposed of either on public land or on private construction sites. (ii) Solid wastes of industrial units are collected and disposed of through public facilities at low-lying public grounds. (iii) Solid wastes cause health hazards through creation of obnoxious smell and harbouring of flies and rodents which act as carriers of diseases like typhoid, diphtheria etc. (iv) The waste causes frequent nuisance when carelessly handled, spread by wind and splattered by rainwater. (v) River pollution from city-based industries and untreated sewage leads to serious health problems downstream. (any three points, or any other relevant point) Measures to overcome: (i) The sewage system should be made more effective with modern technology. (ii) Local self-government/municipalities/corporations (Nagar Nigam) should be more responsible towards solid waste management. (iii) Cleanliness drives can be conducted at frequent intervals in all sectors for positive reinforcement. (any two measures, or any other relevant point)

questions.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
questions.text: (b) Suggest any five measures to solve the problem of land degradation in India.

answer.text: (b) Measures to solve the problem of land degradation in India: (i) Afforestation should be undertaken to control soil erosion, desertification etc. (ii) Irrigational methods should be used judiciously to avoid water logging, salinisation and alkalisation of the soil. (iii) To improve the productive capacity of the land and soil quality, use organic farming or other scientific methods of farming. (iv) Shifting cultivation should be banned. (v) The watershed management programme should be encouraged in degraded land areas to achieve sustainable development. (vi) Mining activities should be monitored. (any five points, or any other relevant point)

questions.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
questions.text: Define water quality. Explain the reasons of deteriorating surface water quality in India.

answer.text: Water quality refers to the purity of water, or water without unwanted foreign substances. Reasons for deteriorating surface water quality in India: (i) water gets polluted by foreign substances such as micro-organisms, chemicals, industrial and other wastes. (ii) water pollutants are also created from natural sources (erosion, landslides, decay and decomposition of plants and animals etc.). (iii) industries produce several undesirable products including industrial wastes, polluted waste water, poisonous gases, chemical residuals, numerous heavy metals, dust, smoke etc. (iv) various types of chemicals used in modern agriculture, such as inorganic fertilisers, pesticides and herbicides, are also pollution-generating components. (v) cultural activities such as pilgrimage, religious fairs, tourism etc. also cause water pollution. (any two points, or any other relevant point)

questions.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
questions.text: Read the given passage carefully and answer the questions that follow : Water Pollution -- Industries produce several undesirable products including industrial wastes, polluted waste water, poisonous gases, chemical residuals, numerous heavy metals, dust, smoke, etc. Most of the industrial wastes are disposed off in running water or lakes. Consequently, poisonous elements reach the reservoirs, rivers and other water bodies, which destroy the bio-system of these waters. Major water polluting industries are leather, pulp and paper, textiles and chemicals. (19.1) Explain how industries are the major contributor of water pollution in India. (19.2) Suggest the way for minimising water pollution. (19.3) Mention two rivers of India which are highly polluted.

answer.text: 19.1 Industries produce industrial waste, poisonous gases, chemical effluents, dust, smoke and heavy metals; when these mix with water they pollute it. 19.2 Ways to minimise water pollution (any one): preventing industrial waste disposal in rivers and lakes to protect their bio-system; preventing agricultural waste like fertilizers and pesticides from reaching fresh water bodies; organising public awareness programmes about the importance of water and the impact of water pollution; encouraging industries and households to reuse treated water. 19.3 Two highly polluted rivers of India: the Ganga/ the Yamuna/ the Sabarmati/ the Gomti/ the Kali/ the Adyar/ the Cooum/ the Vaigai/ the Musi (any two).

questions.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
questions.text: (a) Explain the causes of air pollution and suggest any three measures to overcome it.

answer.text: (a) Causes of air pollution (any two points): increasing use of varieties of fuels as a source of energy has marked a increase in emission of toxic gases into the atmosphere, resulting in pollution of air; combustion of fossil fuels, mining and industries are the main sources of air pollution; solid waste and sewage disposal are also responsible for air pollution; these processes release oxides of sulphur and nitrogen, hydrocarbons, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, lead and asbestos. Measures to overcome air pollution (any three): use of non-conventional sources of energy; control over mining and deforestation; use of pollution-free fuel in industries; increase the height of chimneys and use smoke stacks/filters/scrubbers; use of electric vehicles; reduce, reuse and recycle waste, and promote sewage treatment plants; more use of public transport.

questions.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
questions.text: (b) Explain the causes of noise pollution and suggest any three measures to overcome it.

answer.text: (b) Causes of noise pollution (any two points): noise pollution refers to a state that is unbearable and uncomfortable to human beings, caused by noise from different sources; the main sources of noise pollution are various factories, mechanised construction and demolition work; automobiles and aircraft are also sources of noise pollution; periodic noise from sirens and loudspeakers used in various programmes associated with community activities; the biggest nuisance is noise produced from traffic. Measures to overcome noise pollution (any three): machinery, equipment and generators should be fitted with silencers; machinery can be redesigned to reduce noise; noise-absorbing material may be used; personal use of earplugs and earphones; factories should not be located near human settlements.

questions.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
questions.text: Read the given passage carefully and answer the questions that follow : Water Pollution -- Water pollution is a source of various water-borne diseases. The diseases commonly caused due to contaminated water are diarrhoea, intestinal worms, hepatitis, etc. The World Health Organization shows that about one-fourth of the communicable diseases in India are water-borne. Though river pollution is common to all rivers, yet pollution of the river Ganga flowing through one of the most populous regions of India has caused great concerns among all. To improve the condition of the river, National Mission for Clean Ganga was initiated. The Namami Gange Programme has been launched for the same. (19.1) Describe the main cause of water pollution. (19.2) Mention any two features of the Namami Gange Programme. (19.3) Explain the impact of water pollution on human health.

answer.text: 19.1 Main cause of water pollution (any one): sewage disposal; urban run-off; toxic effluents from industries; run-off over cultivated lands; nuclear power plants. 19.2 Two features of the Namami Gange Programme (any two): it was launched to improve the condition of the river Ganga by effectively controlling pollution; developing sewerage treatment systems in towns; monitoring of industrial effluents; development of river front; afforestation along the bank to increase biodiversity. 19.3 Impact of water pollution on human health (any one): it is a source of various water-borne diseases; diseases commonly caused due to contaminated water are diarrhoea, intestinal worms, hepatitis, etc.; about one-fourth of the communicable diseases in India are water-borne.

questions.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
questions.text: Explain the main causes of air pollution in India. Suggest measures to solve the problem.

answer.text: Causes of air pollution (any two): combustion of fossil fuels; industries and mining; solid waste and sewage disposal. Measures to solve air pollution (any three): use of renewable sources of energy; use of public transport; reduce use of fossil fuels; planting trees; proper management of solid waste and sewage disposal; generate public awareness.

questions.chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
questions.text: Read the given passage carefully and answer the questions that follow : Water Pollution -- Various types of chemicals used in modern agriculture such as inorganic fertilisers, pesticides and herbicides are pollution generating components. These chemicals are washed down to rivers, lakes and tanks. These chemicals also infiltrate the soil to reach the ground water. Fertiliser induces an increase in the nitrate content of surface waters. Manufacturing and improper domestic waste disposal also cause water pollution in India. (18.1) Explain the role of agricultural practices in water pollution. (18.2) How can we check water pollution by changing agricultural practices ? (18.3) Suggest any two ways to reduce water pollution.
questions.topic: Urban Waste Disposal and Solid Waste

answer.text: 18.1 The chemicals used in modern agriculture, such as chemical fertilizers, herbicides and insecticides, are pollution-generating components; when they mix with water they generate pollution. 18.2 Water pollution can be checked by changing agricultural practices, such as through organic farming. 18.3 Two ways to reduce water pollution: recycle used water; treat polluted water before releasing it.
